domains.name: Advanced NLP in Practice
domains.summary: Advanced applied NLP: reproducible text pipelines, sentence embeddings and similarity search, sequence-model practice with span NER and label quality, LLMs as disciplined components, and hybrid information retrieval. Independent study; confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: The shredded contract
scenarios.situation: A RAG system over legal contracts chunks documents into fixed 512-token windows with no overlap. Retrieved passages regularly start or end mid-sentence, and the generator cites fragments that misrepresent the clause they came from. The embedding model tests fine on benchmarks.
choices: Chunk on linguistic boundaries — sentences or paragraphs — with overlap between adjacent chunks, and keep small metadata (section heading, page) on each chunk. Fixed token windows shred the discourse structure the generator needs to quote faithfully.
Increase chunk size to 2048 tokens: bigger windows always help.
Switch to a larger embedding model: the vectors are the problem.
Retrieve more chunks (top-20 instead of top-5): recall fixes everything.
scenarios.why: Retrieval quality is bounded by chunk quality: a perfect embedding of a severed sentence still retrieves a severed sentence. Overlap preserves cross-boundary context, and boundary-aware splitting keeps each chunk self-contained enough to cite. The embedding benchmark was measuring the wrong thing — chunk integrity, not vector quality.
scenarios.hint: If a cited passage starts mid-sentence, is the failure in the embedding, the retrieval, or the chunking — and which one decides what text the generator can see?

scenarios.title: Similar but useless
scenarios.situation: Dense retrieval over a support knowledge base returns passages that paraphrase the user's question beautifully — but do not contain the answer. Cosine similarity is high; task success is low. The team proposes a bigger embedding model.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right diagnosis and fix?
choices: Semantic similarity is not task relevance: embeddings rank 'sounds like the question' above 'answers the question.' Fix with hybrid retrieval (BM25 for lexical precision plus dense for paraphrase), a cross-encoder reranker on the top candidates, and evaluation with recall@k on your own queries — not embedding benchmarks.
Use a bigger embedding model: scale fixes relevance.
L2-normalize the vectors harder: the metric is miscalibrated.
Cosine similarity is the wrong metric: switch to Euclidean distance.
scenarios.why: Embedding benchmarks measure paraphrase similarity, but your task is answer retrieval — different objective, different failure mode. BM25 catches exact terms (error codes, product names) that dense models blur; rerankers score query-passage pairs jointly and consistently beat bi-encoder ranking on precision. Evaluate on your queries or you are optimizing a proxy.
scenarios.hint: The top result paraphrases the question instead of answering it — what does that tell you about what the similarity score is actually measuring?

scenarios.title: The 0.78 ceiling
scenarios.situation: A custom NER model for medical entities plateaus at 0.78 F1 across architectures: BiLSTM-CRF, fine-tuned BERT, larger BERT — all land within a point of each other. The team wants to try a 10x larger model next.
scenarios.prompt: What should they investigate before scaling up?
choices: Label quality: when every architecture plateaus at the same score, the ceiling is usually the annotations. Measure inter-annotator agreement, adjudicate disagreements, and audit a sample of 'errors' — many will be defensible predictions punished by noisy or inconsistent gold labels.
Scale to the 10x model: capacity is the only remaining lever.
Train for 100 epochs: the models are undertrained.
Add more dropout: regularization will break the ceiling.
scenarios.why: Architecture-invariant plateaus are the signature of a data ceiling, not a model ceiling. A model cannot systematically beat the consistency of its own supervision — if two annotators agree only 80% of the time, 0.78 F1 may already be at the achievable limit. The highest-ROI work is adjudication guidelines and span-boundary conventions, not parameters.
scenarios.hint: If three very different architectures all stop at the same score, is the bottleneck more likely in the models — which differ — or in the thing they share?

scenarios.title: The inventive extractor
scenarios.situation: A zero-shot LLM extracts invoice fields (vendor, date, total) into JSON. On 5% of documents it outputs fields that do not appear anywhere in the source text — plausible-looking vendor names and totals. Lowering temperature to 0 did not eliminate it.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make extraction trustworthy?
choices: Constrain and verify: use structured/constrained output (JSON schema), then verify every extracted span against the source document — reject or flag anything not found verbatim. For critical fields, add a hybrid verifier: rules or a second model that checks source grounding. Temperature 0 reduces sampling noise; it does not stop confabulation.
Lower the temperature further: temperature is the only lever.
Use a bigger model: scale eliminates hallucination.
Write a better prompt: prompt engineering fixes extraction.
scenarios.why: Extraction is a grounding task, and LLMs generate rather than copy by default — the failure mode is structural, not a tuning detail. Schema constraints fix the shape; source-span verification fixes the content. The hybrid pattern (LLM proposes, verifier disposes) is how production extraction pipelines earn trust on money fields.
scenarios.hint: The model outputs a total that appears nowhere in the invoice — which step in your pipeline could have caught that, and why didn't temperature fix it?

scenarios.title: The case of XJ-4500
scenarios.situation: Hybrid search evaluation shows dense retrieval missing queries containing exact product codes like 'XJ-4500' — the embedding blurs the code into generic 'product' semantics — while BM25 alone misses paraphrased questions ('my device won't charge' vs 'charging failure troubleshooting'). Each method fails a different query slice.
choices: Keep both and fuse: BM25 for lexical precision on exact tokens (codes, names, error strings) plus dense retrieval for paraphrase and semantics, fused with reciprocal rank fusion or a learned combination, then a reranker on top. Neither method covers both slices; the hybrid exists because their failure modes are complementary.
Retrain the embeddings on product codes: dense retrieval must do everything.
BM25 is obsolete: delete it and tune the dense model harder.
Use dense retrieval only: lexical match is a legacy concern.
scenarios.why: This is the canonical hybrid-search argument: lexical methods excel at rare exact tokens (their IDF weighting is built for it) while dense methods excel at meaning-preserving paraphrase. Deleting either one reintroduces its failure slice. Fusion plus reranking is the standard production stack for exactly this reason.
scenarios.hint: Which query slice does each method win — exact codes or paraphrases — and what does that imply about deleting one of them?

scenarios.title: The labeling buyout
scenarios.situation: Leadership proposes replacing the annotation team with LLM labeling for a 200k-document classification project: 'ten times faster, one-tenth the cost.' A pilot shows 92% agreement with gold labels on easy cases but systematic errors on the ambiguous edge cases that matter most to the business.
choices: Run the quality audit, not the cost math, first: measure LLM-vs-gold agreement sliced by difficulty, keep human adjudication for edge cases and a gold validation set, and present the tradeoff table (cost, latency, error rate per slice). LLM labeling is a force multiplier for the easy majority — not a wholesale replacement where errors are expensive.
Approve the buyout: 92% agreement is good enough for everything.
Reject LLM labeling entirely: machines cannot label.
Use few-shot prompts and ship: prompting fixes the edge cases.
scenarios.why: The pilot's own numbers argue against the buyout: agreement is high where labels are cheap and low where they are valuable. The professional move is the hybrid — LLM first pass, human review on low-confidence and high-stakes slices, and a permanent gold set to detect drift. Present it as a tradeoff table so leadership decides with eyes open.
scenarios.hint: Where do the LLM's errors concentrate — the cheap easy cases or the expensive edge cases — and what does that do to the 'one-tenth the cost' claim?

scenarios.title: The 0.78 ceiling
scenarios.situation: Your classifier plateaus at 0.78 F1 across architectures.
choices: Error analysis on the failures — the ceiling is usually data, not architecture
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Architecture-invariant plateaus signal data/label issues — analyze errors before scaling models.

scenarios.title: The similar-but-useless
scenarios.situation: Embeddings rank paraphrases well but fail your task.
choices: Task mismatch — generic similarity ≠ your objective; fine-tune or task-specific eval
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Off-the-shelf embedding similarity optimizes paraphrase, not your task — align training/eval to the actual objective.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Nlp Advanced as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Advanced NLP in Practice Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Advanced NLP in Practice is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Advanced NLP in Practice?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Advanced NLP in Practice issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Advanced NLP in Practice is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Advanced NLP in Practice supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Advanced NLP in Practice failure in Nlp Advanced.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Advanced NLP in Practice
evidence: All Advanced NLP in Practice components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Transformers Deep Dive
domains.description: Architecture, variants, and scaling of transformers.

scenarios.title: The architecture pick
scenarios.situation: Classify support tickets into 20 categories.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Classification needs deep bidirectional context, not generation — encoder-only models are the efficient, accurate choice.

scenarios.title: The OOM
scenarios.situation: Attention OOMs at 64k context.
choices: FlashAttention + KV cache — IO-aware exact attention plus inference caching
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. FlashAttention computes exact attention in SRAM tiles (no approximation); KV caching avoids recomputation. The standard fix stack.

scenarios.title: The Chinchilla check
scenarios.situation: A 70B model trained on 300B tokens underperforms.
choices: Undertrained — Chinchilla suggests ~1.4T tokens for 70B; data-starved
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 300B tokens for 70B params is ~4 tokens/param vs the ~20 recommended — the model is data-starved, not too large.

scenarios.title: The emergence question
scenarios.situation: Few-shot ability appears only past 10B params.
choices: Emergent ability — capability discovered at scale, not explicitly programmed
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Emergence: qualitative new capabilities arising from scale — a core scaling-laws phenomenon.

scenarios.title: The block sketch
scenarios.situation: Whiteboard the transformer block.
choices: Multi-head attention + FFN + residuals + layer norm — all four
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The block needs all four: attention (mixing), FFN (capacity), residuals (gradient flow), norms (stability).

scenarios.title: The positional pick
scenarios.situation: Need 128k context with extrapolation.
choices: RoPE with scaling — rotary positions extrapolate better than learned
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. RoPE (rotary) with position interpolation/scaling is the modern standard for long-context extrapolation.

scenarios.title: The pretraining pick
scenarios.situation: Build embeddings for semantic search.
choices: Bidirectional (masked LM style) — rich context both directions for representations
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Embedding quality comes from bidirectional context; causal models see only the past.

scenarios.title: The FFN surprise
scenarios.situation: Ablation shows the FFN matters more than expected.
choices: FFNs hold ~2/3 of parameters — they are key-value memories, not afterthoughts
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The feed-forward sublayers contain most parameters and act as learned key-value memories — attention routes, FFNs store.

domains.name: Attention Mechanisms
domains.description: How attention works, visualized and computed.

scenarios.title: The retrieval analogy
scenarios.situation: Explain attention to a database engineer.
choices: Differentiable retrieval: Query searches Keys, returns weighted Values
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Q/K/V maps exactly to query/index/records — the metaphor that makes attention click for DB minds.

scenarios.title: The missing scale
scenarios.situation: Attention outputs saturate; gradients vanish.
choices: Missing √d_k scaling — unscaled dot products grow with dimension and saturate softmax
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. QK^T grows with √d_k; without scaling, softmax saturates and gradients die. The scale factor is load-bearing.

scenarios.title: The cheating model
scenarios.situation: A causal LM gets suspiciously good validation.
choices: Causal mask — future positions may be visible; verify masking
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Suspiciously good causal LM = masking bug until proven otherwise. Verify with tiny examples.

scenarios.title: The head count
scenarios.situation: 16 heads vs 8 heads, same d_model — no gain.
choices: Head redundancy — many heads learn similar patterns; ablate before adding
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Pruning studies show head redundancy is common; more heads is not free capacity.

scenarios.title: The cross attention
scenarios.situation: In translation, where does the decoder see the source?
choices: Cross-attention: decoder queries attend to encoder K/V
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Cross-attention is the bridge: decoder queries over encoder keys/values at every layer.

scenarios.title: The uniform head
scenarios.situation: One head's weights are near-uniform everywhere.
choices: Uninformative/uncertain head — candidate for pruning or investigation
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Uniform attention = the head found nothing to focus on; sharp patterns indicate decisive heads.

scenarios.title: The long-context fix
scenarios.situation: Need 10x longer context, same memory.
choices: FlashAttention + sliding window / linear variants — exact-fast or approximate
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The efficiency stack: FlashAttention (exact, IO-aware) plus architectural options (sliding window, linear) for extreme lengths.

domains.name: LLM Training
domains.description: Pretraining at scale: data, objectives, infrastructure.

scenarios.title: The data edge
scenarios.situation: Two teams, same architecture — one wins big.
choices: Data quality/curation — dedup, filtering, mixing dominate at fixed architecture
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. At fixed architecture and compute, data curation is the highest-leverage differentiator.

scenarios.title: The contamination
scenarios.situation: Benchmark scores look amazing but users disagree.
choices: Test contamination — eval data leaked into training; dedupe against evals
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Inflated benchmarks with poor real performance is the contamination signature — dedupe training against eval sets.

scenarios.title: The parallel pick
scenarios.situation: 70B model, 64 GPUs, OOM with DDP.
choices: 3D parallelism: ZeRO/tensor/pipeline — shard model states, not just data
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. DDP replicates full states; 70B needs sharding — ZeRO for optimizer states, tensor/pipeline for the model itself.

scenarios.title: The spike
scenarios.situation: Loss spikes to NaN at step 50k.
choices: Check gradient clipping, LR schedule, and recent batches; resume from last good checkpoint
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systematic: clipping? LR? bad batch? Then resume from checkpoint — which is why you checkpoint often.

scenarios.title: The tokenizer regret
scenarios.situation: Non-English users complain about slow, costly responses.
choices: High tokenizer fertility for their languages — more tokens per word = slower + pricier
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Fertility disparities tax some languages with 2-3x tokens — evaluate tokenizers multilingually before training.

scenarios.title: The budget
scenarios.situation: Propose training 13B on 260B tokens.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The 6ND estimate turns proposals into budgets — required before spending.

scenarios.title: The bf16 pick
scenarios.situation: fp16 training overflows.
choices: bf16 — wider exponent range avoids overflow; standard for LLM training
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. bf16's exponent range handles LLM activation magnitudes; it is the modern default over fp16.

domains.name: Fine-Tuning & Alignment
domains.description: SFT, RLHF, DPO: making models helpful and safe.

scenarios.title: The LIMA lesson
scenarios.situation: 1k curated pairs beat 100k noisy ones.
choices: SFT data quality dominates quantity — curate ruthlessly
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The LIMA finding: alignment is about teaching format with excellent examples, not drowning in mediocre ones.

scenarios.title: The reward hack
scenarios.situation: RLHF model gives long, flattering, empty answers.
choices: Reward hacking — gaming the helpfulness proxy (verbosity, sycophancy)
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Proxies get gamed: length and flattery correlate with human preference ratings without being helpful.

scenarios.title: The DPO pick
scenarios.situation: Small team, preference data, no RL expertise.
choices: DPO — direct preference optimization without separate reward model or PPO
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. DPO's simplicity (no reward model, no PPO) fits small teams with preference data.

scenarios.title: The new-facts fallacy
scenarios.situation: SFT on company docs; model still hallucinates facts.
choices: SFT teaches format, not reliable knowledge — ground with RAG or pretraining
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. SFT shapes style/behavior; factual grounding comes from retrieval (RAG) or pretraining. Don't expect memorization from fine-tuning.

scenarios.title: The KL anchor
scenarios.situation: PPO policy drifts into repetitive nonsense.
choices: KL penalty to the SFT reference — anchors the policy during optimization
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The KL term keeps the policy near the reference; without it, reward maximization drifts off-distribution.

scenarios.title: The eval triad
scenarios.situation: Model is helpful but hallucinates confidently.
choices: Honesty evals — calibration and hallucination rates, not just helpfulness
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The triad is helpful/harmless/honest — optimizing helpfulness alone can degrade honesty. Evaluate all three.

scenarios.title: The contamination 2
scenarios.situation: Fine-tune data includes benchmark questions.
choices: Decontamination failure — tuned-on-test inflates scores meaninglessly
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Training on eval items is the oldest evaluation sin — decontaminate fine-tuning data against all evals.

domains.name: Prompt Engineering
domains.description: Systematic prompting: few-shot, CoT, structured outputs.

scenarios.title: The vague prompt
scenarios.situation: 'Handle customer complaints well.'
choices: Specify: role, task, constraints, format, examples — prompts are specs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Vague verbs produce vague outputs; the anatomy (role/task/context/constraints/format/examples) makes behavior predictable.

scenarios.title: The few-shot fail
scenarios.situation: 10 examples, still inconsistent.
choices: Curate: 3-5 perfect diverse examples with edge cases — quality over quantity
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Example quality and diversity dominate count; persistent failure after curation signals fine-tuning need.

scenarios.title: The math problem
scenarios.situation: Model fails multi-step arithmetic.
choices: Chain-of-thought — elicit intermediate steps; verify each
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. CoT decomposes the leap into checkable steps — the standard fix for reasoning failures.

scenarios.title: The parse error
scenarios.situation: Pipeline breaks on free-text model output.
choices: Structured outputs (JSON mode) + validation + retry — never string-parse free text
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Constrain to schema, validate automatically, retry with errors fed back — the robust pattern.

scenarios.title: The regression
scenarios.situation: A prompt tweak broke 3 old cases.
choices: Golden set + prompt CI — version prompts, test every change
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Prompts are code: golden sets catch regressions, versioning enables rollback, CI enforces it.

scenarios.title: The self-consistency
scenarios.situation: One CoT chain gives a wrong answer.
choices: Sample multiple chains, majority vote — compute for accuracy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Self-consistency: diverse reasoning paths vote — errors average out, at higher compute cost.

scenarios.title: The system prompt
scenarios.situation: Behavior drifts across sessions.
choices: System prompt with persistent role/rules — versioned and tested
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. System prompts set persistent behavior; version and test them like code.

domains.name: RAG Systems
domains.description: Retrieval-augmented generation: grounding LLMs in your data.

scenarios.title: The grounding need
scenarios.situation: LLM must answer from company docs, updated weekly.
choices: RAG — retrieve fresh chunks, generate with citations; no retraining needed
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Weekly-changing private data is RAG's design center: index updates are cheap, answers stay fresh and cited.

scenarios.title: The chunk fail
scenarios.situation: Retrieval returns irrelevant chunks.
choices: Chunking strategy — boundaries and size decide what embeddings represent
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Bad chunks poison everything downstream; fix boundaries/size/overlap before touching the model.

scenarios.title: The keyword miss
scenarios.situation: Dense retrieval misses exact product codes.
choices: Hybrid retrieval: dense + BM25 — keywords catch exact terms
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Dense embeddings blur exact tokens; BM25 fusion catches product codes, names, IDs.

scenarios.title: The confident fabrication
scenarios.situation: RAG answers with no supporting chunk.
choices: Demand citations + allow abstention — 'answer only from context, else say so'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Ungrounded generation defeats RAG's purpose; citations + abstention enforce honesty.

scenarios.title: The eval gap
scenarios.situation: Users complain but metrics look fine.
choices: Human E2E evaluation on real questions — automated metrics miss nuance
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Component metrics can look fine while E2E fails; human ratings on real queries are the ground truth.

scenarios.title: The stale index
scenarios.situation: Docs updated; RAG answers from old versions.
choices: Incremental re-indexing pipeline — ingest → chunk → embed on doc change
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Freshness needs a pipeline: watch for changes, re-chunk, re-embed incrementally.

scenarios.title: The rerank win
scenarios.situation: Top-5 has the answer at position 4; LLM misses it.
choices: Reranker — cross-encoder reorders top-k precisely; cheap accuracy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Reranking is the highest-ROI RAG upgrade: precise scoring on a small candidate set.

domains.name: Evaluation & Metrics
domains.description: Measuring NLP: from BLEU to human preference.

scenarios.title: The BLEU trap
scenarios.situation: BLEU up 5 points, humans prefer the old system.
choices: BLEU correlates weakly — human eval is gold; report both with caveats
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Automatic metrics approximate; human judgment decides. Divergences are signals, not noise.

scenarios.title: The judge bias
scenarios.situation: LLM judge prefers longer answers.
choices: Rubrics + blind randomized order + length controls + human calibration
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Known judge biases (verbosity, position, self-preference) need protocol defenses and calibration.

scenarios.title: The kappa check
scenarios.situation: Annotators agree at κ=0.2.
choices: Guidelines are broken — pilot, rewrite, retrain annotators
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Near-chance agreement indicts the task design, not the people — fix guidelines first.

scenarios.title: The benchmark pick
scenarios.situation: Evaluate a medical summarizer.
choices: Domain benchmarks + human clinician review — match eval to task risk
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. High-stakes domains need domain benchmarks plus expert human review — generic suites miss the risks.

scenarios.title: The contamination check
scenarios.situation: A model aces a 2021 benchmark.
choices: Check training cutoff and canary strings — pre-cutoff training may include the test
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Contamination checks (cutoffs, canaries, novel probes) separate real capability from memorization.

scenarios.title: The A/B peek
scenarios.situation: Peeking at results daily, stopping when significant.
choices: Optional stopping inflates false positives — pre-register size and criteria
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unadjusted peeking breaks statistical guarantees; pre-register sample size and stopping rules.

scenarios.title: The pairwise pick
scenarios.situation: Rate summaries 1-5 vs A/B choice.
choices: Pairwise A/B — comparative judgments are more reliable than absolute scales
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Humans compare better than they calibrate absolute scales — pairwise wins on reliability.

domains.name: Multilingual NLP
domains.description: Beyond English: cross-lingual transfer and low-resource.

scenarios.title: The transfer test
scenarios.situation: Fine-tuned XLM-R on English NER; deploy to Swahili.
choices: Per-language evaluation — transfer gaps are the norm, measure them
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Cross-lingual transfer varies by language; per-language eval reveals the gaps averages hide.

scenarios.title: The fertility tax
scenarios.situation: Turkish users pay 3x per request vs English.
choices: Tokenizer fertility — more tokens per Turkish word = more cost and latency
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Subword fertility disparities directly tax some languages — a tokenizer fairness issue with dollar costs.

scenarios.title: The low-resource plan
scenarios.situation: Build NER for Quechua with 200 labeled sentences.
choices: Multilingual base + translate-train + the 200 gold for eval — the low-resource playbook
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The playbook: transfer from multilingual base, translate-train for volume, reserve gold native data for honest eval.

scenarios.title: The idiom fail
scenarios.situation: MT renders 'break a leg' literally into German.
choices: Idioms need cultural mapping, not literal translation — localization > translation
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Idioms are cultural, not compositional — they need mapped equivalents, a localization problem.

scenarios.title: The code-switch
scenarios.situation: Users mix Spanish and English mid-sentence; the bot fails.
choices: Train/evaluate on code-switched data — real usage patterns
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Code-switching is normal multilingual behavior — systems must handle it, not punish it.

scenarios.title: The COMET call
scenarios.situation: BLEU says system A wins; humans prefer B.
choices: COMET/human — neural metrics and human judgment over BLEU for MT quality
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. BLEU's n-gram counting misses meaning; COMET (neural) plus human eval is the modern standard.

scenarios.title: The community ask
scenarios.situation: You need Amharic eval data.
choices: Partner with speaker communities (Masakhane-style) — collaborate, don't extract
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Community partnership produces better data and is the ethical standard — collaborate, compensate, credit.

scenarios.title: The 4-bit pick
scenarios.situation: Deploy 70B on 2×80GB GPUs.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 4-bit quantization brings 70B to ~35-40GB — fitting 2×80GB with room for KV cache.

scenarios.title: The throughput gap
scenarios.situation: Naive serving handles 2 req/s; need 20.
choices: vLLM + continuous batching — 10x+ throughput via PagedAttention
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Continuous batching + PagedAttention is the standard 10x throughput unlock — before buying hardware.

scenarios.title: The TTFT complaint
scenarios.situation: Users say the bot feels slow to start.
choices: TTFT (time to first token) — optimize prefill, consider speculative decoding
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Perceived responsiveness = TTFT; optimize prefill (caching, smaller prefill) and consider speculative decoding.

scenarios.title: The routing win
scenarios.situation: 80% of queries are easy; 20% need the big model.
choices: Route: small model first, escalate uncertain/hard queries — cost/quality frontier
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Routing matches cost to difficulty — most queries cheap, hard ones get quality.

scenarios.title: The cache saving
scenarios.situation: RAG system repeats the same long context.
choices: Prefix caching — reuse computed KV for repeated contexts
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Repeated prefixes are pure waste; prompt caching reuses the computation directly.

scenarios.title: The distill call
scenarios.situation: Need teacher quality at 10% latency.
choices: Distillation — student mimics teacher on soft targets

lessons.title: Advanced NLP in Practice — Core concepts
concepts: Pipelines are reproducibility contracts: cleaning decisions, tokenization choices, and chunking strategy must be versioned together, because a silent change in any one of them shifts everything downstream.

Sentence embeddings turn meaning into geometry, but similarity is not relevance: evaluate embeddings on your task (recall@k on your queries), never on a generic benchmark, and expect paraphrase-similar non-answers.

NER is span prediction, not token classification in spirit: boundary conventions decide your F1 as much as the model does, and label quality — measured by inter-annotator agreement — is the ceiling no architecture tunes past.

LLMs are strong NLP components under discipline: zero/few-shot for the easy majority, structured extraction with schema constraints, and LLM labeling only with a human-audited gold set and slice-aware agreement metrics.

Retrieval is a stack, not a model: BM25 for lexical precision, dense retrieval for paraphrase, hybrid fusion for both, and a cross-encoder reranker for precision — each layer covering the last one's failure slice.

Active learning spends the labeling budget where it matters: label the uncertain and the disagreeing, adjudicate edge cases with humans, and keep a frozen gold set so you can detect drift instead of debating it.

example.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # small, fast, honest baseline
docs = [
    "How do I reset my password?",
    "Password reset instructions for locked accounts",
    "What is the refund policy for annual plans?",
    "Refund eligibility and timelines",
]
embs = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)

# Similarity search: rank docs for a query.
q = model.encode(["I forgot my login credentials"], normalize_embeddings=True)
scores = cosine_similarity(q, embs)[0]
for doc, s in sorted(zip(docs, scores), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"{s:.3f}  {doc}")

# Topic discovery: cluster the embedding space.
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(embs)
print(labels)  # expect password docs together, refund docs together

# The discipline the snippet does NOT show: evaluate recall@k on YOUR
# queries, and add BM25 + a reranker before calling this production.
example.walkthrough: This is the working core of modern applied NLP: one small sentence-embedding model gives you similarity search and clustering in twenty lines. Normalized embeddings make cosine similarity a dot product, so ranking is cheap and exact. Clustering the same vectors surfaces topics without any labels — the 'topic discovery' use case. The closing comment is the lesson's real point: the snippet is a baseline, and production adds hybrid retrieval, reranking, and task evaluation — the stack from scenario 5, not just the vectors.

pitfalls: Common trap: evaluating embeddings on a public benchmark instead of your queries — benchmark similarity and task relevance are different objectives.
Common trap: chunking on fixed token windows — shredded sentences produce untrustworthy citations no reranker can repair.
Common trap: treating LLM-extracted fields as grounded facts — verify every extracted span against the source document.
Common trap: scaling the model past an architecture-invariant plateau — when BiLSTM, BERT, and larger BERT all stop at the same F1, audit the labels.

lessons.title: Transformer Anatomy
concepts: Encoder-decoder (original), encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT) — three architectural families.
Core block: multi-head self-attention + feed-forward network + residual connections + layer norm.
Positional encoding: injects order information — sinusoidal, learned, or rotary (RoPE).
Scaling: performance follows power laws in parameters, data, compute — the bitter lesson of scale.

example.code:

  x → MultiHeadAttn → +x → LayerNorm → FFN → +x → LayerNorm
  Repeat N times. That is (almost) the whole model.

pitfalls: Attention-only thinking — the FFN holds 2/3 of parameters.
Ignoring residuals/norms — training collapses without them.

GPT: autoregressive decoder — generation, few-shot, chat. T5: text-to-text unified framework.

Pick by task: understanding → encoder; generation → decoder; seq2seq → encoder-decoder.

Encoder for open generation — wrong tool.

lessons.title: Pretraining Objectives
concepts: Masked LM (BERT): predict masked tokens — bidirectional context.
Causal LM (GPT): predict next token — the scaling workhorse.
Span corruption (T5), replaced token detection (ELECTRA) — efficiency variants.
Objective shapes representations: bidirectional for understanding, causal for generation.

example.code:
OBJECTIVE → STRENGTH:
  Masked LM → deep bidirectional context
  Causal LM → fluent generation at scale
  RTD (ELECTRA) → sample-efficient training
example.walkthrough: The objective IS the inductive bias — choose deliberately.

pitfalls: One objective for everything — match to the downstream task.
Ignoring efficiency variants at small scale.

lessons.title: Scaling Laws and Compute
concepts: Kaplan/Hoffmann scaling: loss ~ power law in N (params), D (data), C (compute) — Chinchilla optimal: scale data with params.
Emergent abilities appear at scale (few-shot, reasoning) — not programmed, discovered.
Compute budgeting: training FLOPs ≈ 6·N·D — plan before you train.
Inference cost matters too: parameters → memory → latency → dollars.

example.code:

  D_optimal ≈ 20 × N tokens
  70B params → ~1.4T tokens
  Undertrained giants waste compute
example.walkthrough: Most 'bigger is better' intuition is really 'better-scaled is better'.

pitfalls: Overtraining small models on huge data — balance per Chinchilla.
Ignoring inference cost — training is once, serving is forever.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.

lessons.title: Efficient Transformers
concepts: Attention is O(n²) — the bottleneck for long contexts.
Solutions: sparse attention, FlashAttention (IO-aware), linear attention, state-space models (Mamba).
KV caching: store keys/values during generation — the standard inference optimization.
Long context: RoPE scaling, sliding windows — extending beyond training length.

example.code:
EFFICIENCY STACK:
  FlashAttention (exact, fast)
  + KV cache (inference)
  + quantization (memory)
  = deployable long-context
example.walkthrough: Efficiency is what turns research models into products.

pitfalls: Naive O(n²) at 100k context — OOM guaranteed.
Ignoring KV cache — 2x+ latency waste.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.

lessons.title: Q, K, V: The Retrieval Metaphor
concepts: Attention = differentiable retrieval: Query asks, Keys index, Values carry content.
Scores: softmax(QK^T / √d_k) — similarity between query and each key, scaled.
Output: weighted sum of Values — the model 'reads' what it attended to.
Scaling by √d_k prevents softmax saturation in high dimensions.

example.code:
ATTENTION:
  scores = QK^T / √d_k
  weights = softmax(scores)
  out = weights · V
example.walkthrough: Think database query: Q=question, K=index, V=records.

pitfalls: Forgetting the scale — unscaled dot products saturate softmax.
Attention = averaging — it is weighted by relevance.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compute one attention head by hand on 3 tokens (tiny dims).

lessons.title: Multi-Head Attention
concepts: Multiple heads = multiple representation subspaces — each head learns different relations.
Heads run in parallel, concatenated, projected — h × d_k = d_model typically.
Different heads specialize: some track syntax, some coreference, some position.
Ablation: many heads are redundant — pruning studies show it.

example.code:
HEADS:
  head_i = Attention(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)
  MultiHead = Concat(heads)W^O
example.walkthrough: More heads ≠ always better — capacity vs redundancy.

pitfalls: Head-count superstition — ablate and measure.
Ignoring head diversity — visualize what each learns.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Read a head-visualization (e.g., BertViz); describe 2 heads' patterns.

lessons.title: Self vs Cross Attention
concepts: Self-attention: Q, K, V from the same sequence — models intra-sequence relations.
Cross-attention: Q from decoder, K/V from encoder — decoder queries source representations.
Causal masking: decoder self-attention masks future positions — no peeking.
Encoder-decoder translation: encoder self-attention → decoder masked self → cross-attention.

example.code:
MASKING:
  Causal: scores[i,j] = -inf for j > i
  Padding: mask pad positions
  Both = correct training
example.walkthrough: Masking bugs are silent killers — verify with tiny examples.

pitfalls: Missing causal mask — the model cheats during training.
Wrong mask at inference — train/inference mismatch.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Draw the causal mask matrix for 4 tokens.

lessons.title: Attention Patterns and Interpretability
concepts: Attention weights are not explanations — but they are useful diagnostics.
Common patterns: local windows, delimiter-focused, positional heads.
Probing: train classifiers on head outputs to see what information they carry.
Use attention to debug: uniform weights = uninformative; sharp = decisive.

example.code:
DEBUG READING:
  Sharp + sensible → healthy
  Uniform → head is dead/uncertain
  Weird spikes → check masking/data
example.walkthrough: Weights inform hypotheses; probes test them.

pitfalls: 'Attention explains' — weights ≠ faithful explanations.
Ignoring heads entirely — they are free diagnostics.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.

lessons.title: Beyond Softmax Attention
concepts: Linear attention: kernelized softmax → O(n) — trades exactness for scale.
FlashAttention: exact attention, IO-aware tiling — the practical standard.
State-space models (Mamba): recurrence with selection — linear-time alternative.
The frontier: keep transformer's quality, escape its quadratic cost.

example.code:
LANDSCAPE:
  Exact+fast: FlashAttention
  Approximate: linear/sparse
  Alternative: SSMs (Mamba)

Ignoring IO — memory movement dominates.

Common pipelines: Common Crawl → dedup → quality filters → domain mixing (code, books, web).
Contamination: test data leaking into training inflates benchmarks — dedupe against eval sets.
Data decisions are the highest-leverage choices in LLM training.

  → Quality filter (classifiers/heuristics)
  → Mix (domains weighted) → Tokenize

lessons.title: Tokenization
concepts: BPE/WordPiece/Unigram: subword vocabularies balancing coverage and sequence length.
Vocab size trade-off: larger vocab → shorter sequences but bigger embedding matrices.
Multilingual tokenizers: watch fertility (tokens per word) — high fertility taxes some languages.
Tokenization is fixed before training — mistakes are expensive.

TOKENIZER CHECKS:
  □ Fertility per language
  □ Round-trip fidelity (decode(encode(x))==x)
  □ Special tokens for your tasks

lessons.title: Distributed Training
concepts: Data parallel: replicate model, shard data — the baseline. ZeRO shards optimizer states to save memory.
Tensor parallel: split layers across GPUs (within node). Pipeline parallel: split layers across stages.
3D parallelism combines all three — the standard for 10B+ training.
Mixed precision (bf16/fp8): halves memory, speeds compute — with loss scaling care.

example.code:
PARALLELISM MAP:
  Data: shard the BATCH
  Tensor: shard the LAYERS (within node)
  Pipeline: shard the DEPTH (across nodes)
example.walkthrough: Choose by bottleneck: memory → ZeRO/tensor; throughput → pipeline.

pitfalls: Naive DDP at 70B — OOM; shard states.
fp16 without care — overflow; prefer bf16.

lessons.title: Stability: Taming Training
concepts: Loss spikes: the bane of LLM training — often from bad batches, LR issues, or precision.
Mitigations: gradient clipping, warmup + cosine decay, careful init, data filtering.
Monitoring: loss, gradient norms, activation stats — watch live, checkpoint often.
Resume-ability: training WILL crash; checkpoint every N steps with full state.

example.code:
STABILITY STACK:
  Clip grads | Warmup LR | Filter data
  Monitor norms | Checkpoint everything
example.walkthrough: A crashed run without checkpoints is weeks lost.

pitfalls: No clipping — one bad batch, one dead run.
Sparse checkpointing — false economy.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.

lessons.title: Compute Budgeting
concepts: FLOPs ≈ 6·N·D (forward+backward) — estimate before spending.
Chinchilla: balance N and D (~20 tokens/param) for compute-optimal training.
Inference is forever: a slightly worse but 2x-cheaper model often wins in production.
Budget template: params × tokens × 6 ÷ GPU-throughput = GPU-hours → dollars.

example.code:
BUDGET:
  7B params × 140B tokens × 6 ≈ 5.9e21 FLOPs
  ÷ A100 (~150 TFLOPS eff) ≈ 11k GPU-hours
example.walkthrough: Do this math before any training proposal.

pitfalls: Training without a budget — the classic blowup.
Ignoring inference cost in the decision.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Budget YOUR capstone-scale training run in GPU-hours and dollars.

lessons.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
concepts: SFT: train on instruction-response pairs — teaches the FORMAT of helpfulness.
Data quality >> quantity: 1k excellent examples beat 100k mediocre ones (LIMA finding).
Full vs parameter-efficient: LoRA/QLoRA update a fraction of weights — the practical default.
SFT teaches style; it does not reliably teach new facts — ground knowledge in pretraining or RAG.

example.code:
SFT RECIPE:
  1. Curate 1-10k high-quality pairs
  2. LoRA (r=8-64) on all linear layers
  3. 1-3 epochs, small LR
  4. Evaluate on held-out tasks
example.walkthrough: LIMA: less is more for alignment — curate ruthlessly.

pitfalls: Massive noisy SFT data — quality over quantity.
Expecting new knowledge from SFT — it teaches format.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Curate 20 SFT pairs for your domain; justify each.

lessons.title: RLHF: Learning from Preferences
concepts: RLHF: SFT → reward model (human preferences) → PPO optimization against the reward.
Reward model: trained on ranked responses — captures 'what humans prefer'.
PPO with KL penalty: stay close to the SFT model while maximizing reward.
Failure modes: reward hacking (gaming the proxy), verbosity bias, sycophancy.

example.code:
RLHF PIPELINE:
  SFT model → collect rankings → train reward model
  → PPO (reward − β·KL) → aligned model
example.walkthrough: The reward model is a proxy — proxies get gamed. Watch for it.

pitfalls: Ignoring reward hacking — evaluate beyond the reward.
No KL penalty — policy drifts into nonsense.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: List 3 ways a model could hack a 'helpfulness' reward.

lessons.title: DPO and Direct Methods
concepts: DPO: optimize directly on preferences without a separate reward model or RL — simpler, stable.
Core idea: the optimal policy has a closed form in terms of preferences — derive the loss directly.
Variants: IPO, KTO, ORPO — the direct-alignment zoo is growing fast.
Trade-off: simpler than RLHF; online/iterative variants still maturing.

example.code:
DPO LOSS (essence):
  Increase margin: log π(chosen) − log π(rejected)
  Anchored to reference model via β
example.walkthrough: DPO is the pragmatic default for preference tuning today.

pitfalls: DPO as magic — data quality still dominates.
No reference anchoring — drift risk.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compare DPO vs RLHF: when would you pick each?

lessons.title: Evals for Alignment
concepts: Helpfulness: task success, instruction following (IFEval), human win-rates.
Harmlessness: refusal of disallowed content, bias benchmarks, red-teaming.
Honesty: calibration, hallucination rates — does it know what it doesn't know?
Evaluate the triad (helpful, harmless, honest) — optimizing one can hurt others.

example.code:
ALIGNMENT EVALS:
  Helpful: IFEval, MT-Bench
  Harmless: red-team suites, bias benchmarks
  Honest: calibration plots, hallucination evals
example.walkthrough: Goodhart's law applies to evals too — diversify.

pitfalls: Single-metric optimization — the triad matters.
Eval-only tuning — hold out truly unseen tests.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick 3 evals for your capstone; justify the mix.

lessons.title: Instruction Tuning Data Curation
concepts: Diversity beats volume: cover task types, difficulties, and styles.
Decontaminate against evals — tuned-on-test is the oldest sin.
Synthetic data: useful but watch for model collapse over generations — mix with human data.
Document the data: sources, filters, licenses — reproducibility and legality.

example.code:
CURATION CHECKLIST:
  □ Diverse tasks/styles
  □ Decontaminated vs evals
  □ License-clean
  □ Quality spot-checked
example.walkthrough: Your fine-tune is only as good as your pairs.

pitfalls: Scraped data without licenses — legal risk.
No decontamination — fake gains.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Audit 50 candidate pairs; keep/drop with reasons.

lessons.title: Prompt Anatomy
concepts: Anatomy: role + task + context + constraints + format + examples.
Specificity wins: 'summarize in 3 bullets under 50 words' beats 'summarize this'.
System prompts set persistent behavior; user prompts carry the task.
Version your prompts — they are code; diff and test them.

example.walkthrough: Write prompts like specs, not wishes.

pitfalls: Vague verbs — 'handle this' means nothing.
No format spec — unparseable outputs.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite 3 vague prompts using the template.

lessons.title: Few-Shot and In-Context Learning
concepts: Few-shot: examples in the prompt teach the pattern — no weight updates.
Example quality > quantity: 3 perfect examples beat 10 sloppy ones.
Order and diversity matter: cover edge cases, not just the easy path.
When few-shot fails consistently → the task needs fine-tuning or RAG.

example.code:
FEW-SHOT DESIGN:
  □ 3-5 diverse examples
  □ Edge cases included
  □ Consistent formatting
  □ Most recent = most similar (recency bias)
example.walkthrough: Few-shot is programming by example — engineer the examples.

pitfalls: 10 random examples — curate, don't dump.
Ignoring failures — persistent misses signal fine-tuning need.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Build a 4-shot prompt for a classification task; test on 20 cases.

lessons.title: Chain-of-Thought and Reasoning
concepts: CoT: 'think step by step' elicits intermediate reasoning — big gains on math/logic.
Zero-shot CoT ('Let's think step by step') vs few-shot CoT (worked examples).
Self-consistency: sample multiple chains, majority vote — trades compute for accuracy.
Faithfulness caveat: chains may rationalize rather than reveal — verify, don't trust blindly.

example.code:
COT PATTERN:
  Q → [step 1] → [step 2] → ... → Answer
  Verify each step independently where possible
example.walkthrough: CoT converts one hard leap into checkable steps.

pitfalls: CoT for everything — overhead without benefit on easy tasks.
Trusting chains blindly — verify the steps.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Solve 5 reasoning problems with and without CoT; compare.

lessons.title: Structured Outputs
concepts: JSON mode / function calling: constrain outputs to schemas — parseable, reliable.
Validate: schema-check every output; retry on failure with the error fed back.
Function calling: describe tools as JSON schemas; the model picks and fills arguments.
Design schemas for the consumer — minimal, typed, documented.

example.code:
ROBUST PATTERN:
  1. Request JSON per schema
  2. Validate
  3. On fail: re-prompt with error
  4. Fallback after N tries
example.walkthrough: Unvalidated LLM output in a pipeline is a bug factory.

pitfalls: String-parsing free text — use structured outputs.
No validation — trust but verify, automatically.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Build a JSON-schema extraction task with validation + retry.

lessons.title: Prompt Testing and Iteration
concepts: Golden sets: 20-100 representative cases with expected outputs — your regression suite.
A/B prompts: change one variable, measure on the golden set.
Track: prompt version, model version, scores — prompts rot as models update.
Automate: CI for prompts on every change — treat like code.

example.code:
PROMPT CI:
  golden set + eval script
  → score per prompt version
  → block regressions
example.walkthrough: If you can't measure it, you can't improve it.

pitfalls: Vibes-based iteration — measure.
No golden set — regressions go unnoticed.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Build a 20-case golden set for one of your prompts.

lessons.title: RAG Architecture
concepts: RAG: retrieve relevant chunks → stuff into prompt → generate grounded answer — hallucination antidote.
Pipeline: ingest → chunk → embed → index → retrieve → rerank → generate → cite.
Why it wins: fresh data without retraining, citations for trust, smaller models suffice.
Failure modes: bad retrieval (garbage in), chunk boundaries, stale index.

example.code:
RAG FLOW:
  Docs → chunks → embeddings → vector DB
  Query → embed → top-k → rerank → prompt → answer + cites
example.walkthrough: RAG is the default answer to 'LLM + our data' — master it.

pitfalls: Skipping eval — RAG has many knobs; measure.
No citations — unverifiable answers.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Diagram the pipeline for your capstone docs.

lessons.title: Chunking Strategies
concepts: Chunking: split docs into retrievable units — size and boundaries decide quality.
Fixed-size: simple, splits mid-thought. Semantic: split on meaning (headings, sections).
Overlap: 10-20% overlap preserves context across boundaries.
Rule: chunks should answer one question each — test by retrieval, not theory.

example.code:
CHUNKING GUIDE:
  Size: 200-500 tokens typical
  Overlap: 10-20%
  Boundaries: semantic > fixed
  Metadata: source, section, date
example.walkthrough: Evaluate chunking by retrieval recall, not aesthetics.

pitfalls: Whole docs as chunks — diluted embeddings.
No overlap — severed context.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Chunk one doc three ways; compare retrieval on 5 queries.

lessons.title: Embeddings and Vector Search
concepts: Embeddings: dense vectors capturing meaning — similarity = relevance.
Models: general (e.g., E5, BGE) vs domain-tuned — match to your corpus.
Indexes: HNSW (fast, memory), IVF (balanced) — the ANN trade-offs.
Hybrid: dense + BM25 keyword — catches exact terms dense misses.

example.code:
RETRIEVAL STACK:
  Embed query → ANN top-50 → rerank top-10
  → feed top-5 to LLM
  Hybrid: + BM25 fusion
example.walkthrough: Hybrid retrieval is the robust default — pure dense misses keywords.

pitfalls: Dense-only on jargon-heavy corpora — BM25 catches exact terms.
No reranker — cheap precision win skipped.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark dense vs hybrid on 20 queries; report recall@5.

lessons.title: Reranking and Generation
concepts: Reranker: cross-encoder scores query-chunk pairs precisely — expensive but accurate on top-k.
Generation: stuff top chunks with citations demanded; instruct 'answer only from context'.
Citation: require [source] markers — verifiability is the point of RAG.
'I don't know': allow abstention when retrieval is weak — honesty over hallucination.

example.code:
GENERATION PROMPT:
  'Answer using ONLY the context. Cite sources [1][2].
   If the answer is not in the context, say so.'
example.walkthrough: Citations turn RAG from demo into trustworthy tool.

pitfalls: No abstention — forced answers hallucinate.
Ignoring rerank — biggest cheap win.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Add citation requirements + abstention to your RAG prompt; test.

lessons.title: Evaluating RAG
concepts: Retrieval metrics: recall@k, MRR — did we find the right chunks?
Generation metrics: faithfulness (supported by context?), answer relevance, citation accuracy.
End-to-end: human preference on real questions — the ultimate test.
RAGAS-style frameworks automate pieces — but sample human review always.

example.code:
RAG EVALS:
  Retrieval: recall@5, MRR
  Generation: faithfulness, relevance
  E2E: human ratings on 50+ queries
example.walkthrough: Evaluate components AND the pipeline — failures localize.

pitfalls: E2E only — can't tell retrieval from generation failures.
No human sample — automated metrics miss nuance.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Build a 30-question eval set for your RAG; score it.

lessons.title: Classical Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, and Limits
concepts: BLEU: n-gram precision for translation — fast, gameable, weakly correlated with quality.
ROUGE: n-gram recall for summarization — same caveats.
F1/accuracy for classification; exact match for extractive QA.
Rule: automatic metrics rank systems roughly; humans judge absolutely.

example.code:
METRIC REALITY:
  BLEU/ROUGE: cheap, approximate
  Human eval: expensive, gold
  LLM-as-judge: middle ground, watch bias
example.walkthrough: Never report BLEU alone as 'quality' — report with caveats.

pitfalls: Metric hacking — optimizing BLEU, degrading quality.
No human sample — flying blind.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compute ROUGE on 5 summaries; compare to your own judgment.

lessons.title: LLM-as-Judge
concepts: Strong LLMs grade outputs — scalable, decent correlation with humans.
Biases: verbosity, position, self-preference — mitigate with rubrics and randomization.
Rubric-based judging: criteria + scale beat 'rate 1-10' vibes.
Calibrate: compare judge vs human on a sample; report agreement.

example.code:
JUDGE PROTOCOL:
  Rubric (criteria, scale)
  → blind, randomized order
  → multiple samples
  → human calibration subset
example.walkthrough: LLM judges are instruments — calibrate them.

pitfalls: Uncalibrated judging — unknown reliability.
Judge = same model family — self-preference.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Judge 20 outputs with a rubric; have a human score 10; compare.

lessons.title: Human Evaluation Done Right
concepts: Design: clear guidelines, examples, pilot — annotators need training.
Agreement: measure inter-annotator agreement (kappa) — low agreement = bad guidelines.
Pairwise > absolute: 'A vs B' is more reliable than 'rate A 1-5'.
Cost control: sample strategically (uncertain cases), not uniformly.

example.code:
HUMAN EVAL:
  Guidelines + examples → pilot → kappa check
  → pairwise comparisons → adjudicate ties
example.walkthrough: Good human eval is a research contribution itself.

pitfalls: No guidelines — annotator chaos.
Ignoring disagreement — it signals bad task design.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write guidelines for rating summaries (1 page).

lessons.title: Benchmarks and Leaderboards
concepts: GLUE/SuperGLUE: NLU suite. MMLU: multitask knowledge. HumanEval: code. HELM: holistic.
Leaderboard dynamics: saturation, contamination, gaming — read critically.
Choose benchmarks matching YOUR task — generic leaderboards mislead.
Contamination checks: canary strings, date cutoffs, novel tests.

example.code:
BENCHMARK LITERACY:
  What does it test? → match to your need
  Saturated? → diminishing signal
  Contaminated? → discount
example.walkthrough: Benchmarks are tools, not verdicts.

pitfalls: Leaderboard worship — single-number thinking.
Ignoring contamination — fake SOTA.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick 3 benchmarks for your capstone; justify each.

lessons.title: A/B Testing in Production
concepts: Offline metrics ≠ online impact — A/B test with real users and business metrics.
Design: randomized, sufficient power, guardrail metrics (latency, cost).
Interleaving for ranking; bandits for continuous optimization.
Ship criteria: statistically significant + practically meaningful.

example.code:
A/B CHECKLIST:
  □ Randomization unit
  □ Power analysis (sample size)
  □ Guardrails (latency, cost, safety)
  □ Pre-registered success criteria
example.walkthrough: Pre-register criteria — no moving goalposts.

pitfalls: Peeking without correction — false positives.
No guardrails — winning metric, broken product.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Design an A/B test for two RAG variants (metrics + size).

lessons.title: Cross-Lingual Transfer
concepts: Multilingual models (mBERT, XLM-R) transfer: fine-tune in English, test in 100 languages.
Transfer works best for: similar tasks, related languages, sufficient pretraining coverage.
Zero-shot gaps: low-resource languages lag — measure per-language, not just average.
Translate-train: machine-translate training data — often beats zero-shot for low-resource.

example.code:
TRANSFER RECIPE:
  1. Fine-tune multilingual model (English data)
  2. Evaluate PER LANGUAGE
  3. Gap? → translate-train or target-language data
example.walkthrough: Report per-language scores — averages hide the gaps that matter.

pitfalls: English-only eval — the average lies.
Assuming transfer is uniform — it is not.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Evaluate an XLM-R model on 5 languages; plot the gaps.

lessons.title: Tokenization Across Languages
concepts: Fertility: tokens per word varies wildly — some languages cost 3x more per word.
Script coverage: ensure the vocab covers your languages' scripts — check, don't assume.
Morphologically rich languages (Turkish, Finnish) need subword granularity.
Tokenizer choice is a fairness choice — it taxes some users more.

example.code:
TOKENIZER AUDIT:
  □ Fertility per target language
  □ Script coverage
  □ Cost impact per language
example.walkthrough: Audit before training — tokenizer regret is expensive.

pitfalls: English fertility only — the standard blind spot.
Ignoring cost disparity — some users pay 3x.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Audit 2 tokenizers on 4 languages; report fertility.

lessons.title: Low-Resource Strategies
concepts: Reality: most languages lack labeled data — work with what exists.
Strategies: cross-lingual transfer, translate-train/test, synthetic data, active learning.
Community data: Masakhane, AmericasNLP — partner with speaker communities.
Evaluate with native speakers — automatic metrics miss cultural fit.

example.code:
LOW-RESOURCE PLAYBOOK:
  1. Transfer from multilingual base
  2. Translate-train pivot
  3. Small native eval set (gold)
  4. Iterate with speakers
example.walkthrough: Partner with communities — don't extract from them.

pitfalls: English-centric design — then 'extend' as afterthought.
No native evaluation — flying blind.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Pick a low-resource language; sketch the playbook for NER.

lessons.title: Machine Translation Today
concepts: NMT: encoder-decoder transformers; LLMs now rival dedicated systems for many pairs.
Quality varies by pair: high-resource pairs are excellent; low-resource lag.
Evaluate with COMET/BLEURT + human — BLEU alone misleads.
Document-level MT: context beyond sentences — the current frontier.

example.code:
MT EVAL:
  Automatic: COMET, BLEURT
  Human: adequacy + fluency
  Both, per language pair
example.walkthrough: Always human-review critical translations — MT errors are confident.

pitfalls: BLEU-only claims — weak signal.
Sentence-only thinking — documents have context.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Compare two MT systems on 20 sentences; judge with COMET + your eyes.

lessons.title: Cultural and Linguistic Nuance
concepts: Language carries culture: idioms, politeness, taboos — translation ≠ localization.
Bias: models reflect training-data cultures; test across cultural contexts.
Code-switching: real users mix languages — handle it, don't punish it.
Inclusive design: involve native speakers from the start, not as QA afterthought.

example.code:
NUANCE CHECKLIST:
  □ Idioms handled?
  □ Politeness levels?
  □ Code-switching OK?
  □ Native-speaker reviewed?
example.walkthrough: Fluency without cultural fit is still failure.

pitfalls: Literal translation of idioms — nonsense.
One-culture testing — bias by omission.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Find 3 idiom failures in an MT system; propose fixes.

lessons.title: Quantization
concepts: Quantization: fewer bits per weight (16→8→4) — less memory, faster inference.
GPTQ/AWQ: 4-bit with minimal accuracy loss — the practical standard.
Trade-offs: extreme quantization hurts perplexity; calibrate on representative data.
Rule: quantize for deployment, evaluate after — never assume.

example.code:
QUANT LADDER:
  fp16 → int8 (easy) → int4 GPTQ/AWQ (standard)
  → 2-bit (research, risky)
example.walkthrough: 4-bit is the current sweet spot for open models.

pitfalls: Quantize-and-hope — always re-evaluate.
Ignoring calibration data — match the domain.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Quantize a 7B model to 4-bit; compare perplexity.

lessons.title: Distillation
concepts: Distillation: train a small student to mimic a large teacher's outputs (or distributions).
Works when: you need teacher quality at student cost — edge, latency SLAs.
Data: teacher labels on unlabeled data — the classic recipe.
Limits: student rarely beats teacher; distill the right teacher.

example.code:
DISTILL RECIPE:
  1. Teacher generates labels/logits
  2. Student trains on soft targets
  3. Evaluate gap; iterate
example.walkthrough: Distillation compresses knowledge, not just weights.

pitfalls: Distilling a weak teacher — garbage in.
Expecting student > teacher — rare.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Distill a classifier to 10% size; measure the gap.

lessons.title: Serving: vLLM, TGI, and Batching
concepts: vLLM (PagedAttention): memory-efficient serving, continuous batching — the open standard.
Continuous batching: pack requests dynamically — 10x+ throughput vs naive.
TGI (HuggingFace): production serving with similar optimizations.
Choose by: throughput needs, hardware, ecosystem fit.

example.code:
SERVING STACK:
  PagedAttention (memory) + continuous batching (throughput)
  + quantization (size) = production
example.walkthrough: Naive HuggingFace generate() is 10x slower than vLLM — know the gap.

pitfalls: No batching in production — throughput collapse.
Ignoring TTFT vs TPOT — different SLOs.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Benchmark naive vs vLLM on 100 requests; report throughput.

lessons.title: Latency and Cost SLOs
concepts: TTFT (time to first token): responsiveness. TPOT (time per output token): streaming smoothness.
Cost: $/1M tokens — track input vs output separately (output costs more).
Trade-offs: bigger model = better quality, worse latency/cost.
Set SLOs first, then pick the smallest model that meets quality bars.

example.code:
SLO TEMPLATE:
  TTFT < 500ms | TPOT < 50ms
  Cost < $X/1M tokens
  Quality ≥ bar on golden set
example.walkthrough: SLOs turn 'fast and cheap' into engineering targets.

pitfalls: Quality-only thinking — latency/cost are product features.
No SLOs — unmeasurable goals.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write SLOs for a customer-support bot.

lessons.title: Caching and Routing
concepts: Prompt caching: reuse prefixes across requests — huge savings for repeated contexts.
Semantic caching: return cached answers for similar queries — watch staleness.
Model routing: small model first, escalate hard queries — cost/quality frontier.
These compound: cache + route + quantize = 10x cost reduction.

example.code:
COST STACK:
  Cache (repeated work) → Route (right-size model)
  → Quantize (smaller) → Batch (throughput)
example.walkthrough: Layer these — each multiplies the savings.

pitfalls: No caching — paying for repeated work.
One model for everything — mispriced.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Estimate savings from caching for your RAG system's repeated contexts.

lessons.title: Bias in Language Models
concepts: Models reflect training data: stereotypes in, stereotypes out — measure, don't assume.
Benchmarks: BBQ, Winogender, CrowS-Pairs — quantify bias, don't hand-wave.
Mitigations: balanced data, debiasing techniques, careful prompting — partial, not solved.
Report bias evals alongside accuracy — both are quality.

example.code:
BIAS EVAL:
  BBQ (QA bias) | Winogender (coreference)
  → measure → mitigate → re-measure
example.walkthrough: If you don't measure it, you ship it.

pitfalls: 'Debiased' claims without evals — prove it.
English-only bias testing — bias is multilingual.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Run a BBQ-style probe on a model; report 3 findings.

lessons.title: Red-Teaming Language Models
concepts: Red-teaming: adversarial probing for harmful outputs — jailbreaks, injections, misuse.
Method: diverse attackers, documented attempts, severity ratings, fix verification.
Prompt injection: untrusted input hijacking instructions — the top LLM app vulnerability.
Red-team before launch and continuously — attackers don't stop.

example.code:
RED-TEAM LOOP:
  Probe → document → rate severity
  → mitigate → verify → repeat
example.walkthrough: Treat red-teaming like pen-testing: adversarial, ongoing.

pitfalls: One-time testing — threats evolve.
Ignoring prompt injection — the #1 app risk.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Attempt 5 jailbreaks on a model; document results.

lessons.title: Privacy and Data Leakage
concepts: Models memorize: PII in training can be extracted — the leakage risk is real.
Mitigations: PII scrubbing, differential privacy, careful data governance.
User data: don't train on it without consent; provide deletion.
Evaluate extraction risk before deploying on sensitive domains.

example.code:
PRIVACY CHECKS:
  □ PII scrubbed from training
  □ Extraction tested
  □ User-data policy clear
  □ Deletion honored
example.walkthrough: Assume memorization — design accordingly.

pitfalls: 'Public data is safe' — PII hides in public text.
No extraction testing — unknown risk.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Write a data policy for an LLM product (1 page).

lessons.title: Responsible Deployment
concepts: Disclose AI involvement — users deserve to know they're talking to a model.
Human oversight for high-stakes: medical, legal, financial — AI assists, humans decide.
Monitoring: track failures, abuse, drift in production — launch is the start.
Incident response for AI: bad outputs need a response plan like security incidents.

example.code:
DEPLOY CHECKLIST:
  □ Disclosure □ Human-in-loop (high-stakes)
  □ Monitoring □ Abuse response plan
example.walkthrough: Deployment ethics is operational, not theoretical.

pitfalls: Silent AI — undisclosed automation erodes trust.
No monitoring — blind to harm.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Draft an AI incident response plan (1 page).

lessons.title: Regulation Landscape
concepts: EU AI Act: risk-based tiers — unacceptable/high/limited/minimal, with obligations per tier.
US: sectoral + executive orders — evolving; track NIST AI RMF.
High-risk uses (hiring, credit, policing) face the strictest requirements.
Build compliant-by-design: documentation, evals, human oversight — ahead of mandates.

example.code:
COMPLIANCE POSTURE:
  Classify your use case by risk tier
  → meet that tier's obligations
  → document everything
example.walkthrough: Regulation rewards the prepared.

pitfalls: Ignoring jurisdiction — deploy globally, comply locally.
No documentation — un-auditable.
Skimming without self-testing — cover the concepts above and recall each aloud before moving on.
lessons.try_it: Classify your capstone under the EU AI Act tiers.

Prerequisites assumed: basic ML, Python, and introductory NLP (tokenization, embeddings).
How to use: domains build progressively — transformers before training, training before alignment.
Capstone ties it together: a real LLM system, evaluated honestly.

labs.title: Hybrid retrieval toy: BM25 plus dense
labs.objective: Build a small hybrid search stack — hand-rolled BM25, sentence-embedding dense retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion — and show measured recall@k on a query set where each method alone fails a slice.
steps: Create lab1.py with 30 short documents on two topics, deliberately including exact codes (e.g. 'XJ-4500') in some and paraphrased descriptions in others.
Implement a compact BM25 scorer from scratch (term frequency, inverse document frequency, length normalization) and rank all 30 docs for 6 test queries.
Add dense retrieval with sentence-transformers: encode docs and queries, rank by cosine similarity.
Fuse both rankings with reciprocal rank fusion and compute recall@5 for BM25-only, dense-only, and fused — print all three numbers.
Identify one query each method wins, and in three sentences explain why the fused ranking covers both failure slices.

checks.hint: Print lines like 'bm25 recall@5 0.XXXX / dense recall@5 0.XXXX / fused recall@5 0.XXXX' so the check can compare all three.

labs.title: Span-F1 evaluator and label audit
labs.objective: Write a span-level NER evaluator, run it on sample gold vs predicted spans, then simulate label noise to show how annotation inconsistency caps measured F1.
steps: Create lab2.py: define 20 gold entity spans (text, start, end, label) over 5 short sentences, and a predicted set with 3 boundary errors, 2 label errors, and 2 misses.
Implement span-level precision, recall, and F1 requiring exact boundary plus label match; print the scores to four decimals.
Now corrupt the gold set: randomly shift 4 span boundaries by one token (simulating annotator disagreement) and re-score the same predictions against the noisy gold.
Print both F1 numbers and compute the gap; in three sentences, explain what this implies about architecture comparisons run on noisy labels.
Draft a three-rule span-boundary convention (e.g. include/exclude articles, handle conjunctions) that would have prevented your simulated disagreements.

checks.hint: Print lines like 'clean-gold F1 0.XXXX / noisy-gold F1 0.XXXX' so the check can see the label-noise effect.
